units.text: 1. When We Say Someone Is Responsible
One Word, Several Processes

An engineer inspects a bridge. A worker installs a component. A director cuts the maintenance budget. A storm strikes the structure. The bridge collapses. The next morning, the public asks who bears responsibility. The question may mean who caused the accident, who should be investigated, who must compensate the victims, or who must ensure that the other bridges do not collapse. A single sentence is trying to do the work of several investigations.

The philosophy of responsibility distinguishes being a cause from being morally accountable. An object can cause a death without being a moral agent. When assessing a person, control and what that person could understand matter, among other things. Nor does an obligation to perform a task coincide with credit or blame for its outcome. Contemporary scholarship separates these questions precisely because they overlap only in part. [ 1 ]

In this book, causal responsibility will mean contributing to an outcome. Retrospective moral responsibility will concern the grounds for praising, criticizing, or blaming someone for what they did or failed to do. Role responsibility will concern the tasks attached to a position: parent, researcher, administrator, employee. Prospective responsibility will concern what must be done from now on. Reparative responsibility will concern restoring, compensating for, or acknowledging harm. These are working distinctions, not sealed compartments of life.

There is also legal liability. It depends on rules, procedures, evidence, and institutional authority. We will not deduce it directly from the book’s moral judgments. An act can be legal and still reprehensible; a moral obligation may not be appropriate for legal enforcement. Asking a friend to be attentive is different from asking the state to punish him for not being a good friend. Conversely, some compensation mechanisms aim to distribute a risk without declaring the person required to pay a bad human being.

We can now take the bridge case apart. The worker installed the component, but perhaps he was given defective material that the inspection required of him could not detect. The financial director never touched the structure, but perhaps she eliminated an inspection she knew was necessary. The engineer may have done everything that could reasonably be asked and still be the person best placed to organize urgent inspections. Her obligation for the next day does not establish her blame for the previous one.

The distinction protects us from two symmetrical injustices. The first is scapegoating: we seek out the person closest to the outcome and place the entire chain of causes in their arms. The second is the disappearance of obligations into complexity: because nobody controlled everything, we conclude that nobody owes anything. Between them lies the difficult work of identifying each person’s contributions, warnings, duties, alternatives, and actual power.

There is also responsibility as a character trait. We call someone responsible when we can rely on them. But trust needs an object. An accountant can be exceptionally consistent in administering a fraud. An official can flawlessly carry out an unjust procedure. Reliability and morality are not identical. To call a person responsible in a richer sense, we must also care about the things for which they consider themselves accountable, not merely the regularity with which they accomplish them.

Finally, publicly accepting responsibility is not necessarily accepting it in practice. “I take responsibility” can precede an explanation, a resignation, reparation, or absolutely nothing. The formula has substance only if it changes the relationship between the speaker and the consequences. Who may ask questions? What information must be provided? What must be corrected? What power may be withdrawn? Responsibility without the possibility of being questioned and without an obligation to change anything risks remaining a verbal ceremony.
Are We the Authors of Our Actions?

Two drivers check a message while driving. Nobody appears in front of the first. A pedestrian crosses in front of the second. The initial negligence is the same; the consequences are radically different. We have reasons to treat the need for reparation differently. But do we have equally strong reasons to believe that the second driver was, at the very moment of choosing, a much worse person?

The debate about moral luck, associated in its contemporary form with Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, begins with this conflict. We want moral assessment to concern what depends on the agent, yet outcomes, circumstances, and even part of the agent’s character depend on factors they did not choose. The problem is not only the luck of avoiding an accident. It is also the luck of never having been placed in a situation that would have exposed our weaknesses. [ 2 ]

We do not know how courageous we are merely because we have not been threatened. We do not know how incorruptible we are merely because nobody has offered us something important. This observation should temper moral triumphalism, not suspend every judgment. Actions remain different. Someone who resisted pressure deserves recognition. But comparing people requires more than comparing their visible outcomes.

The question goes deeper still. We did not choose our genes, family, language, or earliest role models. If every choice comes from a personality shaped by prior causes, where does genuine authorship begin? Incompatibilists hold that certain forms of determination threaten the freedom responsibility requires. Compatibilists argue that an action can be free in a relevant sense if it arises from a person’s deliberation and ability to respond to reasons, even in a causally governed world. Simply invoking chance does not solve the problem either: a random movement does not thereby become my choice. [ 1 ]

Let us take an example without spectacular metaphysics. One person turns on a tap because he wants water. Another turns it on after someone physically forces his hand. The final movement may be identical. But the explanations differ in how the person participates in producing it. In the first case, his information, purpose, and deliberation play a role. In the second, they are bypassed. Even if both episodes have causes, the difference remains relevant to how we can demand explanations and change behavior.

This does not establish the existence of absolute desert, independent of a person’s entire history. It establishes only that the statement “everything has causes” does not by itself erase every distinction between coercion, reflection, manipulation, negligence, and intention. We can reject the idea that someone deserves suffering merely to restore the universe’s metaphysical balance while still preserving the protection of victims, the establishment of facts, demands for explanations, and the obligation to make reparation.

Knowledge matters to such demands too. Not having known may be an excuse, but sometimes the failure to check is precisely the problem. The literature calls this the epistemic dimension of responsibility. Not all ignorance is culpable: we must investigate whether the person could have recognized the need to become informed and whether they had reasonable means to do so. A standard that demands everyone foresee every consequence no longer distinguishes a human being from an oracle. [ 3 ]

Imagine two people providing the same false information. One repeats, in good faith, a credible announcement they had no reason to suspect. The other ignores three warnings because the truth would undermine their advantage. Correcting the information is necessary in both cases. The reproach need not be identical. Here we see the advantage of differentiated responsibility: it can demand repair without inventing identical blame, and criticize the avoidance of knowledge without punishing the mind’s inevitable limitations.
Real, Invented, or Both?

We cannot put responsibility in a container. But neither a promise, a financial debt, nor a marriage is that kind of object. The absence of a separate physical body does not make a concept unreal. Some realities exist through shared rules and relationships. They can change lives even though they would not exist in a universe without beings capable of understanding them.

Yet the fact that a rule exists socially does not establish that it is just. A community can rigorously enforce an absurd obligation. The sociological reality of attributed guilt does not guarantee the moral truth of the accusation. We must therefore separate two questions: do people actually organize the world through responsibility? And are the particular ways they distribute it justified? The first can be investigated through observation, documents, experiments, and history. The second requires arguments about reasons, rights, interests, and the acceptable treatment of persons.

Suppose a village considers a thief’s family guilty of the theft, although its members neither helped nor knew anything about it. The norm is socially real. It produces shame, exclusion, and perhaps violence. But precisely its reality makes it open to criticism. We do not need to deny the practice’s existence to deny its legitimacy. Much of the moral progress we can imagine consists in this separation: institutions exist, but they are not sacred merely because they function.

Moral realism, constructivism, and various forms of antirealism offer divergent answers about the ultimate status of moral judgments. Broadly speaking, realism holds that moral truths exist; many of its forms regard them as independent of our approval. For a constructivist, their justification depends on how they would emerge from an appropriate rational procedure, not on mere whim. An antirealist may explain moral language through attitudes and practices without accepting independent moral properties. These families contain internal disagreements, and some forms of constructivism may be compatible with realism; the labels do not settle the issue. [ 4 ]

We can, however, move forward without claiming to have settled the ontology of all morality. If someone accepts that their own suffering matters, we can ask them to explain why another person’s similar suffering should count for nothing. If they accept that other people’s promises create legitimate expectations for them, we can ask them to explain why their own promises should be decorative. These questions do not logically convert every egoist. They expose the cost and asymmetry of that person’s position. Moral philosophy has no proof that can force everyone to care; it has ways of making a refusal to care harder to hide behind an appearance of neutrality.

I propose treating responsibility as a justifiable relationship between an agent, something that depends on them, and other beings whose interests are affected. “Justifiable” is essential. Not every expectation others have becomes my obligation. A group may demand obedience, a partner may demand that I give up my entire life, an institution may demand silence. The demand must be assessed, not merely recorded.

This working definition rejects both a universe in which every pain automatically conceals a sin and a social universe in which nobody owes anybody anything. It leaves room for unchosen obligations: a dependent child has signed no contract with its parents; someone accidentally struck may need help from the person who struck them; an administrator assumes tasks generated by their position. Not having chosen the whole situation does not mean that all our reactions are equally justifiable.

Responsibility is therefore real at least as a social practice and as a problem of justification. Whether it also exists in the stronger sense of independent moral truths remains a philosophical dispute. But nobody can eliminate the problem merely by saying the word “invented.” Bridges are constructed too. The relevant question is whether they hold, whom they allow to cross, and who is crushed when they collapse.
